Zhang Guozhen 張國珍 was registered in Yongchuan County, Chongqing Prefecture, Sichuan, in a civilian household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he had the courtesy name Tingzhong, ranked first among his brothers, and was aged thirty-three, born on the third day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Taiquan; his grandfather, Yi; his father, Yinghan; and his mother, née Wu. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Guoyao and Guoqing. He married a woman née Cui and subsequently women née Song and née Sun. He placed thirteenth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 112th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lu Jiaqing 盧嘉慶 was registered in Xiangfu County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, in a civilian household. A prefectural government school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he had the courtesy name Jifu, ranked first among his brothers, and was aged twenty-five, born on the thirteenth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Gang; his grandfather, Cheng; and his father, Jian. His father's former wife was née Liu, and his mother was née Zhu. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Jiaxiang, Jiayou, and Jiayan. He married a woman née Xie and subsequently a woman née Yang. He placed seventy-third in the Henan Provincial Examination and 400th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ding Shengshi 丁盛世 was registered in Shouzhang County, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, in a military household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Rites, he had the courtesy name Zifeng, ranked first among his brothers, and was aged thirty-seven, born on the fourteenth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shu; his grandfather, Tai; his father, Keming, an Assistant Instructor; and his mother, née Liu. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Zhishi and Anshi. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed thirty-fifth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 139th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Keli 王可立 was registered in Lai'an County, Chuzhou, in the directly administered metropolitan region, in a civilian household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he had the courtesy name Zizhong, ranked third among his brothers, and was aged thirty-seven, born on the fourteenth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Guang, an Assistant Prefect; his grandfather, Anqing; and his father, Zheng. His father's former wife was née Chen, and his mother was née Zhang. His mother was living, and his father was deceased. His elder brothers were Kejiu and Keda. He married a woman née Li and subsequently a woman née Zou. He placed 121st in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 375th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zhang Chong 張翀, courtesy name Ziyi, was registered in a military household of the Liuzhou Guard in Liuzhou Prefecture, Guangxi. A prefectural school student specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he was fifth in birth order, aged twenty-nine, and born on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Shen; his grandfather, Shan; and his father, Quan, an Assistant Instructor. His mother was née Li. His mother alone was still living. His elder brother Yi was a District Magistrate, and his wife was née Wang. He ranked ninth in the Guangxi Provincial Examination and forty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Zhen 劉溱, courtesy name Zigang, was registered in a military household in Anyang County, Zhangde Prefecture, Henan. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Documents, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-three, and born on the second day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Jie, a Commander in a Military and Police Office; his grandfather, Jian; and his father, Lu, a Ceremonial Escort. His legal mother was the Lady of Yangdi County, and his birth mother was née Hou. The entry records his mother as surviving and his father as deceased. His younger brother was Wei, and his wife was née Zhang. He ranked twenty-first in the Henan Provincial Examination and 373rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhu Chang 朱裳, courtesy name Zekun, was registered in a military household in Wen County, Huaiqing Prefecture, Henan. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Changes, he was second in birth order, aged thirty-three, and born on the ninth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Hao; his grandfather, Qi; his father, Zongren; and his mother, née Zheng. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Yi, his younger brother was Gun, and his wife was née Zhao. He ranked thirty-third in the Henan Provincial Examination and 334th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhao Zonggui 趙宗軌, courtesy name Xiqing, was registered in a salt-producing household in Cangzhou, Hejian Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region (Zhili). A subprefectural school student specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-three, and born on the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Xuan; his grandfather, Zirong; and his father, Ji, an Assistant Instructor. His father's former wife was née Cheng, and his mother was née Qiang. His mother alone was still living. His younger brother was Zongding, and his wife was née Wang. He ranked ninety-fourth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and sixty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

This means that the duties of both superior and subordinate entail principles that are exceedingly difficult to fulfill. Even rulers of dim ability often compare with those above [?]; why should one not exert oneself? Receiving the accumulated blessings bequeathed by my late imperial father and mother, I have reverently received High Heaven’s illustrious mandate, chosen and entrusted with the office of ruler…

translation_en: …at ease while ministers toil: all can say this, yet very few earnestly put it into practice in heart and person. The sage’s teaching that one should first act upon what one intends to say is treated as empty words. You assembled scholars have not yet taken office, and your minds and aspirations remain clear and unclouded. You have long been hearing and observing, and surely have well-founded judgments that will not change. Set them forth directly in your essays as your response.

title: 嘉靖三十二年進士登科錄
text:
臣陳謹
臣對臣聞帝王之御世也致治于無虞者君臣
相得之功保治于無疆者君臣交儆之助何者
天之立君所以任繼天之責君之得臣所以弘
子民之道是君臣之分雖殊而克艱之司則一
使非有相得之情則分隔而志不通無以究經
綸之蘊非有交儆之益則面從而心日弛難以
致一德之孚惟夫君立其綱臣任其事則心不
勞而萬幾日理君虛其受臣獻其誠則志不怠
而化理維新夫然則君臣道合所以謨明弼諧
===
者有成功上下情聯所以輔理承化者有偉績
鞏國祚于苞桑之固措天下於泰山之安者端
在是矣欽惟
皇帝陛下以
剛健中正之資備
文武聖神之德光昭
大統克纘
鴻基啓中興之令圖開太平之昌祚蓋粹乎位斯
道之中而建維皇之極者也臣竊伏草茅遙被
治化久矣迺者叨有司之薦得以與

者有成功上下情聯所以輔理參化者有偉績

皇上帝陛下以
剛健中正之資備
文武聖神之德光昭
大統克纘
鴻基啓中興之令圖開太平之昌祚蓋辟乎位斯

治化久矣頋者叨有司之薦得以與
punctuated:
臣陳謹。

臣對：臣聞帝王之御世也，致治于無虞者，君臣相得之功；保治于無疆者，君臣交儆之助。何者？天之立君，所以任繼天之責；君之得臣，所以弘子民之道。是君臣之分雖殊，而克艱之司則一。使非有相得之情，則分隔而志不通，無以究經綸之蘊；非有交儆之益，則面從而心日弛，難以致一德之孚。惟夫君立其綱，臣任其事，則心不勞而萬幾日理；君虛其受，臣獻其誠，則志不怠而化理維新。夫然，則君臣道合，所以謨明弼諧者有成功；上下情聯，所以輔理承化者有偉績。鞏國祚于苞桑之固，措天下於泰山之安者，端在是矣。

欽惟皇帝陛下，以剛健中正之資，備文武聖神之德，光昭大統，克纘鴻基，啓中興之令圖，開太平之昌祚，蓋粹乎位斯道之中，而建維皇之極者也。臣竊伏草茅，遙被治化久矣。迺者叨有司之薦，得以與
translation_en:
Your servant Chen Jin.

Your servant replies: I have heard that, when emperors and kings govern the world, bringing it to order free from peril is the achievement of ruler and ministers understanding one another; preserving that order without end is aided by ruler and ministers admonishing one another. Why is this? Heaven establishes a ruler to entrust him with the responsibility of carrying on Heaven’s work; the ruler obtains ministers to extend the Way of caring for the people as his children. Thus, although ruler and ministers differ in station, their charge to overcome difficulties is one. Without mutual understanding, their stations would separate them and their intentions would not communicate, leaving them unable to realize the full resources of statecraft. Without the benefit of mutual admonition, there would be outward compliance while inward resolve grew daily more lax, making it difficult to achieve the trust born of unity in virtue. Only when the ruler establishes the guiding principles and ministers undertake the affairs of government can his mind remain unwearied while the myriad matters of state are put in order each day. When the ruler receives counsel with an open mind and ministers offer their sincerity, his resolve does not slacken, and moral transformation and good government are continually renewed. In this way, ruler and ministers unite in the Way, and clear deliberation and harmonious assistance achieve their purpose; those above and below are joined in feeling, and assistance in government and the furtherance of moral transformation produce great accomplishments. Securing the dynasty’s fortunes as firmly as a deeply rooted clump of mulberry trees, and setting the realm in a stability like that of Mount Tai, depend precisely upon this.

I reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor, endowed with strength, vigor, balance, and uprightness, possesses the virtues of civil refinement, martial prowess, sageliness, and spiritual insight. You have gloriously illuminated the great imperial succession and worthily continued its magnificent foundations, initiating an admirable plan for dynastic resurgence and opening an era of flourishing fortunes and great peace. Indeed, you stand with perfect purity at the center of this Way and establish the supreme imperial standard. Your servant, dwelling obscurely among the common people, has long received from afar the benefits of your transforming government. Recently, through the undeserved recommendation of the responsible officials, I have been enabled to participate in …

title: 嘉靖三十二年進士登科錄
text:
大廷之對而
聖策首及於君臣克艱之言臣譾陋粗疎之見誠不
足以裨
國論之萬一然一得之愚敢披忠悃就
陛下所問及者而敬陳之嘗考之書曰亶聰明作元
后元后作民父母言天之立君所以代天而施
長民之政也詩曰藹藹王多吉人維君子命媚
于庶人言君之得臣所以體君而敷惠民之澤
也君代天而為之子是故所居者天之位也所
宣者天之言也所行者天之工也以上天化育
之所不及而寄之於君則君之責亦甚重矣臣
體君而為之用是故所食者君之禄也所治者
君之民也所理者君之事也以人君分理之重
寄而托之於臣則臣之責亦不易矣是以克艱
厥后克艱厥臣誠有如大禹所論者在昔唐虞
之世代天者有放勳重華之聖其克艱之任為
不負矣而當時輔弼之臣隨事分理同心以協
其謀都俞吁咈儆戒以成其美是以上下交而
德業成而時雍風動之休至今稱盛治也三代
之時在上者有祗台建中之君純德敬義之主

八廷之對而
聖策首及於君臣克艱之言臣謭陋寡識不
足以裨
國論之萬一然一得之愚敢披忠悃就
陛下所問及者而敬陳之嘗考之書曰亶聰明作元
后元后作民父母言天之立君所以代天而施
長民之政也詩曰藹藹王多吉人維君子命媚
于庶人言君之得臣所以體君而敷惠民之澤
也君代天而爲之子是故所居者天之位也所
宣者天之言也所行者天之工也以上天化育
===
之所不及而寄之於君則君之責亦甚重矣臣
體君而爲之用是故所食者君之祿也所治者
君之民也所理者君之事也以人君分理之重
寄而托之於臣則臣之責亦不易矣是以克艱
厥后克艱厥臣誠有如大禹所論者在昔唐虞
之世代天者有放勳重華之聖其克艱之任爲
不負矣而當時輔弼之臣隨事分理同心以協
其謀都俞吁咈儆戒以成其美是以上下交而
德業成而時雍風動之休至今稱盛治也三代
之時在上者有祇台建中之君純德敬義之主
punctuated: 大廷之對，而聖策首及於君臣克艱之言。臣譾陋粗疎之見，誠不足以裨國論之萬一。然一得之愚，敢披忠悃，就陛下所問及者而敬陳之。嘗考之，《書》曰：「亶聰明作元后，元后作民父母。」言天之立君，所以代天而施長民之政也。《詩》曰：「藹藹王多吉人，維君子命，媚于庶人。」言君之得臣，所以體君而敷惠民之澤也。君代天而為之子，是故所居者天之位也，所宣者天之言也，所行者天之工也。以上天化育之所不及而寄之於君，則君之責亦甚重矣。臣體君而為之用，是故所食者君之禄也，所治者君之民也，所理者君之事也。以人君分理之重寄而托之於臣，則臣之責亦不易矣。是以克艱厥后，克艱厥臣，誠有如大禹所論者。在昔唐虞之世，代天者有放勳、重華之聖，其克艱之任為不負矣。而當時輔弼之臣，隨事分理，同心以協其謀，都俞吁咈，儆戒以成其美。是以上下交而德業成，而時雍風動之休，至今稱盛治也。三代之時，在上者有祗台建中之君、純德敬義之主
translation_en:
…to present my response at the great court, and Your Majesty’s policy question begins by addressing the words concerning rulers and ministers recognizing the difficulty of their duties. My shallow and crude views are truly insufficient to contribute even the slightest benefit to deliberations on affairs of state. Yet, with whatever single insight a fool may possess, I venture to lay bare my loyal sincerity and respectfully address the matters Your Majesty has asked about.

I have examined the Book of Documents, which says: “One who is truly perceptive and enlightened becomes the sovereign; the sovereign becomes the father and mother of the people.” This means that Heaven establishes a ruler to act on its behalf in governing the people. The Book of Odes says: “Abundant are the king’s many worthy men [?]; it is the noble men’s charge to show love to the common people.” This means that the ruler obtains ministers so that they may embody his intentions and spread his beneficence among the people. The ruler acts on Heaven’s behalf as its son. Thus, the position he occupies is Heaven’s position; the words he proclaims are Heaven’s words; and the work he performs is Heaven’s work. Since whatever Heaven’s transforming and nurturing power cannot reach is entrusted to the ruler, the ruler’s responsibility is indeed exceedingly weighty. Ministers embody the ruler’s intentions and serve him. Thus, the stipends they receive are the ruler’s stipends; the people they govern are the ruler’s people; and the affairs they administer are the ruler’s affairs. Since the weighty charge of sharing the ruler’s administration is entrusted to ministers, their responsibility is likewise no easy one. Therefore, the ruler must recognize the difficulty of being a ruler, and ministers the difficulty of being ministers, just as the Great Yu indeed explained.

In the ancient age of Tang and Yu, those who acted on Heaven’s behalf possessed the sageliness of Fangxun and Chonghua, and did not fail in their charge to recognize the difficulty of their duties. The assisting ministers of that time divided administrative responsibilities according to the matters at hand and united their hearts to coordinate their counsels. Through approval and assent, objection and dissent, they admonished their rulers and brought their virtues to fulfillment. Thus, those above and below communicated with one another, and virtuous achievements were accomplished. The blessings of universal harmony and transformation spreading like the wind are praised to this day as exemplary government. In the age of the Three Dynasties, those who ruled included the sovereign who said, “Revere me,” and established the Mean, and the ruler of pure virtue who revered righteousness…

其克艱之責可以繼唐虞而稱美矣而其贊襄
之佐亦皆相知以心形迹不累相濟以道飭勵
無疑是以君臣孚而世道泰而雍熈太和之治
後世言盛治者稱三代不衰也嗣是而降去唐
虞三代遠矣安馬上之習而新語之獻陸賈徒
肆乎空言尚經術之名而曲學之諛公孫得容
于阿世盡言無隱魏徵之正直似矣而大綱未
正不能措其主於三代之隆論語半部趙普之
治平似矣而國勢不振不能致其君於雍熈之
美甚至假經術以經世務而上慕唐虞之言徒
為欺君罔上之策其相得之情雖或時一見焉
而交儆之道則槩乎其未有聞也求其相得交
儆以盡克艱之任君逸臣勞以成致治之美者
不有見於
今日乎洪惟我
太祖高皇帝繼天立極應人啓統正華夷之大分復
萬古之綱常一時經制之謨真足以並唐虞而
邁三代矣觀其書大學衍義于廡壁而謂學士
宋濂曰朕之為君上畏天地下畏兆民兢兢業
業不敢自逸大哉

translation_en:
…In fulfilling their responsibility to grapple with the difficulties of rulership, they could succeed Tang and Yu and earn equal praise. Their assisting ministers likewise understood them at heart, unencumbered by outward formalities; they aided one another through the Way, with no misgivings about mutual admonition and encouragement. Thus ruler and ministers trusted one another, and the realm enjoyed peace. So harmonious and tranquil was their government that later generations, in speaking of flourishing rule, never ceased to praise the Three Dynasties.
Thereafter, the age grew far removed from Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties. When the ruler remained content with the habits of governing from horseback, Lu Jia’s presentation of New Discourses (Xin yu) amounted merely to empty words. When the ruler prized the reputation of classical learning, Gongsun gained acceptance by flattering his age through distorted scholarship. In speaking fully and concealing nothing, Wei Zheng seemed to embody uprightness; yet the fundamental principles remained unrectified, and he could not raise his sovereign to the flourishing rule of the Three Dynasties. With half of the Analects, Zhao Pu seemed to achieve peace and order; yet the strength of the state failed to revive, and he could not bring his ruler to the excellence of harmonious government. Some even borrowed classical learning to manage worldly affairs, while their lofty professions of admiration for Tang and Yu served merely as devices for deceiving their sovereign. Although mutual sympathy between ruler and minister might occasionally appear, scarcely anything was heard of their mutually admonishing one another. If we seek those who understand and admonish one another so as fully to discharge their arduous responsibilities, with the ruler at ease and the ministers laboring to achieve excellent government, do we not find them today?
We reverently reflect upon our Emperor Taizu Gao, who succeeded Heaven in establishing the supreme standard and responded to the people in founding the dynasty. He set right the great distinction between the Chinese and the barbarians and restored the cardinal bonds and constant virtues for all time. His plans for institutions and government were truly sufficient to equal Tang and Yu and surpass the Three Dynasties. Consider how he had the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning (Daxue yanyi) inscribed on a corridor wall and said to Academician Song Lian: “As ruler, above I stand in awe of Heaven and Earth, and below I stand in awe of the myriad people. title: 嘉靖三十二年進士登科錄
text:
皇言其深明人君克艱之任者乎臣甞伏讀
聖製諸書而知
聖祖所以盡其克艱之道者至矣論道主乎執中稽
治本乎堯舜至於
祖訓之制尤所以示貽謀燕翼之道者自持守以至
國政而大綱具張自禮儀以至供用而萬目備
舉他若
聖政之記通訓之章大明日曆之編存心省躬之録
其脩身體道立綱陳紀所以遺萬世
聖子神孫之太平者詳且悉矣
===
聖作物覩而一時名世之臣雲從景附以弼成大業
先幾如劉基學行如宋濂徐達之沉毅端重常
遇春之剛毅勇畧李文忠之器量沉闊沐英之
謀慮深遠至於陶安之議論無雙王禕之學兼
體用上下之間咸有一德信非漢唐宋之君臣
所能及也
列聖相承重熙累洽而明良相遇之盛盖先後而有
光矣我
皇上以憲
天法

punctuated:
皇言！其深明人君克艱之任者乎！臣甞伏讀聖製諸書，而知聖祖所以盡其克艱之道者至矣。論道主乎執中，稽治本乎堯舜。至於《祖訓》之制，尤所以示貽謀燕翼之道者。自持守以至國政，而大綱具張；自禮儀以至供用，而萬目備舉。他若《聖政》之記、《通訓》之章、《大明日曆》之編、《存心省躬》之録，其脩身體道、立綱陳紀，所以遺萬世聖子神孫之太平者，詳且悉矣。
聖作物覩，而一時名世之臣雲從景附，以弼成大業。先幾如劉基，學行如宋濂，徐達之沉毅端重，常遇春之剛毅勇畧，李文忠之器量沉闊，沐英之謀慮深遠，至於陶安之議論無雙，王禕之學兼體用，上下之間咸有一德，信非漢唐宋之君臣所能及也。
列聖相承，重熙累洽，而明良相遇之盛，盖先後而有光矣。我皇上以憲天法
translation_en:
…imperial words! How profoundly they reveal the ruler’s responsibility to meet difficulties! Your servant has reverently read the various imperially authored books and learned how consummately the sagely founder fulfilled the way of meeting difficulties. In discussing the Way, he placed chief emphasis on holding to the mean; in examining good government, he took Yao and Shun as his foundation. His compilation of the Ancestral Instructions especially demonstrated the way to leave sound plans for his descendants and secure their well-being. From personal discipline to affairs of state, all the principal guidelines were set forth; from ritual observances to provisions and expenditure, every detail was addressed. Other works include the Records of Sagely Governance, the General Instructions, the Daily Record of the Great Ming, and the Record of Preserving the Mind and Examining Oneself. Their teachings on cultivating oneself and embodying the Way, establishing fundamental principles and setting forth rules—thereby bequeathing peace to his sagely sons and divine grandsons for countless generations—are detailed and comprehensive.
The sage arose, and all beheld him. The eminent ministers of that age followed him like clouds and attended him like shadows, assisting him in accomplishing his great enterprise. There were Liu Ji, who perceived events before they unfolded; Song Lian, distinguished in learning and conduct; Xu Da, composed, resolute, upright, and dignified; Chang Yuchun, firm and determined, courageous and skilled in strategy; Li Wenzhong, profound and broad in capacity; and Mu Ying, far-reaching in his plans and deliberations. There were also Tao An, unrivalled in deliberation, and Wang Yi, whose learning embraced both underlying principles and practical application. Ruler and ministers shared a single virtue. Truly, the rulers and ministers of the Han, Tang, and Song could not equal them.
Successive sage emperors inherited the throne, adding brilliance to brilliance and prosperity to prosperity. The flourishing partnership of enlightened rulers and worthy ministers shone from one reign to the next. Our emperor, with the intention of emulating Heaven and taking as his model…

title: 嘉靖三十二年進士登科錄
text:
祖之心懋高明光大之學
敬一傳心仁孝持念祭祀必致其精誠憂勤先謹
乎天戒則天德之純有以豫内聖之體矣
勵精圖治誠心愛民戚畹不得恃恩近侍不得干
紀躬籍田之耕下賑恤之詔則王道之備有以
達外王之用矣
陛下撫日中之地而勤克艱之思信足以副
上天簡畀之明命而民胞物與未嘗少忽者也
德意所及萬方之黎庶皆將樂樂利利思觀德化之
成而况為之臣者尚忍負之乎是以中外臣工
===
莫不滌志慮以承休德大臣法小臣廉三孤弘
化六卿分職至於分藩專城秉旄仗節文武之
臣日思效忠而宣力者皆曰將以翼
九重恭己之化矣然而
聖制有曰為臣者無克艱之思每懐欺於謗甚至勾
沙漠以為骨肉但逞劫主之逆不顧胞與之害此
其至大者臣請得而言之臣聞之曰治世非無小
人也難乎其為小人亂世非無君子也難乎其
為君子明于此者可以知其故矣昔唐堯之世
賢聖滿朝而有方命之鯀野無遺賢有虞之治

祖之心，懋高明光大之學，敬一傳心，仁孝持念。祭祀必致其精誠，憂勤先謹乎天戒，則天德之純有以豫内聖之體矣。勵精圖治，誠心愛民，戚畹不得恃恩，近侍不得干紀；躬籍田之耕，下賑恤之詔，則王道之備有以達外王之用矣。陛下撫日中之地，而勤克艱之思，信足以副上天簡畀之明命，而民胞物與未嘗少忽者也。德意所及，萬方之黎庶皆將樂樂利利，思觀德化之成，而况為之臣者，尚忍負之乎？是以中外臣工莫不滌志慮以承休德，大臣法，小臣廉，三孤弘化，六卿分職，至於分藩專城、秉旄仗節文武之臣，日思效忠而宣力者，皆曰將以翼九重恭己之化矣。
然而聖制有曰：「為臣者無克艱之思，每懐欺於謗，甚至勾沙漠以為骨肉，但逞劫主之逆，不顧胞與之害。」此其至大者，臣請得而言之。臣聞之曰：「治世非無小人也，難乎其為小人；亂世非無君子也，難乎其為君子。」明于此者，可以知其故矣。昔唐堯之世，賢聖滿朝，而有方命之鯀；野無遺賢，有虞之治
translation_en:
…with a resolve to emulate the ancestors, diligently cultivates learning that is lofty, enlightened, luminous, and expansive. Through reverent singleness of purpose, Your Majesty transmits the teaching of the mind, keeping benevolence and filial piety constantly in thought. In sacrifices, you invariably devote the utmost purity and sincerity; in anxious diligence, you attend first to Heaven’s admonitions. Thus the purity of heavenly virtue serves to establish [?] the substance of inner sagehood. You exert yourself to achieve good government and sincerely love the people. Imperial relatives may not presume upon favor, and attendants may not violate the rules. You personally plow the imperial field and issue edicts for relief. Thus the completeness of the Kingly Way brings the functioning of outward kingship to fruition. Your Majesty rules the land beneath the midday sun, diligently mindful of overcoming difficulties. This truly suffices to fulfill the luminous mandate by which Heaven selected and entrusted you; never for a moment have you neglected to regard the people as siblings and all creatures as companions. Wherever your virtuous intentions reach, the common people throughout the realm will all rejoice in their joys and benefit from their benefits, hoping to witness the fulfillment of your transforming virtue. How, then, could those who serve as your ministers bear to betray you? Accordingly, officials at court and throughout the realm all purify their intentions and thoughts to receive your excellent virtue. Great ministers observe the laws; lesser ministers remain incorruptible. The Three Junior Dukes extend your transforming influence, and the Six Ministers discharge their respective duties. Civil and military officials administering regions and cities or bearing command banners and credentials daily consider how to show loyalty and exert their strength. All declare that they seek thereby to assist the transforming influence Your Majesty exercises through reverent self-discipline within the palace.
Yet Your Majesty’s decree states: “Those who serve as ministers give no thought to overcoming difficulties, but constantly harbor deceit and slander [?]. They even collude with those of the desert, treating them as their own flesh and blood. They seek only to carry out the rebellious act of coercing their sovereign, heedless of the harm to the people and creatures who are their siblings and companions.” This is the gravest matter; your servant begs leave to discuss it. Your servant has heard it said: “An orderly age is not without petty men, but it is difficult for them to act as petty men. A disordered age is not without gentlemen, but it is difficult for them to act as gentlemen.” Those who understand this can grasp the reason. In ancient times, during the age of Tang Yao, worthies and sages filled the court, yet there was Gun, who defied commands. No worthy remained overlooked in the countryside, and the government of Youyu …

title: 嘉靖三十二年進士登科錄
text:
至矣而比周為黨復有一共工焉堯舜不以鯀
與共工而盡疑乎在朝之輔佐而後世之尚論
者亦未嘗以此而病堯舜官人之明也
陛下以堯舜之心為心以堯舜之治為治而在廷之
臣復以堯舜其
君為己責堯舜不能無共工伯鯀則小人之病國雖
盛世豈能必其無哉故今天下之臣其在
朝廷輦轂豈無秉義竭忠之臣然而違上所好朋
家作仇者未盡無也其在百工庶府豈無亮采
惠疇之臣然而納賄招權誣上自恣者未盡無
===
也其在內臺司諫豈無彰順匡過之臣然而附
和面從黨同伐異者未盡無也其在軍門督府
豈無鷹揚效死之臣然而剛愎自用貪殘少恩
者未盡無也其在藩臬守令豈無旬宣和惠之
臣然而違道干譽尸祿養望者未盡無也甚者
剥民之膏脂以肥其家竊君之榮寵以張其勢
掠人美以市恩恣己私以敗度者未盡無也人
之度量雖智愚相越存乎御之何如耳陸贄曰
漢高稟大度故其時多瑰傑不羈之材漢武好
英風故其時富瓌詭立名之士漢宣精吏治故

者未盡無也其在藩臬守令豈無旬宣和惠之
臣然而違道干譽尸祿養望者未盡無也甚者
剝民之膏脂以肥其家竊君之榮寵以張其勢
掠人美以市恩恣已私以敗度者未盡無也人
之度量雖智愚相越存乎御之何如耳陸贄曰
漢高稟大度故其時多瑰傑不羈之材漢武好
英風故其時富瓌詭立名之士漢宣精吏治故
punctuated: 至矣，而比周為黨，復有一共工焉。堯舜不以鯀與共工而盡疑乎在朝之輔佐，而後世之尚論者亦未嘗以此而病堯舜官人之明也。陛下以堯舜之心為心，以堯舜之治為治，而在廷之臣復以堯舜其君為己責。堯舜不能無共工、伯鯀，則小人之病國，雖盛世豈能必其無哉？故今天下之臣，其在朝廷輦轂，豈無秉義竭忠之臣？然而違上所好，朋家作仇者，未盡無也。其在百工庶府，豈無亮采惠疇之臣？然而納賄招權，誣上自恣者，未盡無也。其在內臺司諫，豈無彰順匡過之臣？然而附和面從，黨同伐異者，未盡無也。其在軍門督府，豈無鷹揚效死之臣？然而剛愎自用，貪殘少恩者，未盡無也。其在藩臬守令，豈無旬宣和惠之臣？然而違道干譽，尸祿養望者，未盡無也。甚者，剥民之膏脂以肥其家，竊君之榮寵以張其勢，掠人美以市恩，恣己私以敗度者，未盡無也。人之度量，雖智愚相越，存乎御之何如耳。陸贄曰：「漢高稟大度，故其時多瑰傑不羈之材；漢武好英風，故其時富瓌詭立名之士；漢宣精吏治，故
translation_en:
…had reached perfection, yet there was still a Gonggong who formed cliques and factions. Yao and Shun did not, on account of Gun and Gonggong, suspect all their assistants at court; nor have later generations, in judging the ancients, ever used this to fault Yao and Shun’s discernment in appointing officials. Your Majesty takes the heart of Yao and Shun as your own heart, and their governance as your own governance; the ministers at court likewise regard making their sovereign a Yao or Shun as their own responsibility. Yet even Yao and Shun could not avoid having a Gonggong or a lord Gun. How, then, can even a flourishing age be certain that no petty men will injure the state?

Thus, among the empire’s ministers today, are there none at court and in the capital who uphold righteousness and exert their utmost loyalty? Yet neither are they entirely free of those who oppose what their sovereign favors and form factions to act as adversaries. Among the officials of the various offices and bureaus, are there none who faithfully discharge their duties and work harmoniously with their colleagues? Yet neither are they entirely free of those who accept bribes, arrogate power, deceive their sovereign, and indulge themselves without restraint. In the Censorate and the remonstrance offices, are there none who make good conduct manifest and correct faults? Yet neither are they entirely free of those who echo others and profess outward obedience, support their own faction, and attack those who differ. In the military commands and supervisory headquarters, are there none who display martial valor and serve unto death? Yet neither are they entirely free of those who are obstinate and self-willed, greedy and cruel, and deficient in kindness. Among provincial administration and surveillance officials, prefects, and magistrates, are there none who carry out their duties throughout their jurisdictions with harmony and benevolence? Yet neither are they entirely free of those who depart from the Way to court praise, draw salaries without performing their duties, and cultivate their reputations. Worse still, there remain those who strip the people of their substance to enrich their own families, steal their sovereign’s honors and favor to expand their own power, appropriate others’ merits to purchase favor, and indulge their private interests to subvert established rules.

Although people differ widely in capacity and in wisdom or folly, what matters is how they are governed. Lu Zhi said: “Emperor Gao of Han possessed great magnanimity; thus his age abounded in outstanding men of unrestrained talent. title: 嘉靖三十二年進士登科錄
text:
其時萃淳良核實之能言下之係乎所率也漢
之三君固非純於王道之主然而御臣有其道
則臣下之趨向隨之而况
聖明之世陋三君於不屑者乎夫君猶盂也臣猶水
也盂圓則水隨以圓盂方則水隨以方惟在
陛下一轉移之間耳臣願
陛下崇寬大之體廣虛受之衷委任而相得益章論
道而交儆不替忠邪當辨而大臣之細過勿詰
可也事理當審而言官之狂戇者勿遽震之威
可也罔上當懲也而事無首尾泛相沿及者勿
槩坐可也陽是陰非臆度附會者可誅也而所
見不同本無意必者勿絶其生還可也託忠賢
以為腹心開言路以廣耳目君有匪懈之誠臣
懷媚上之衷面從後言如舜之所以戒禹也無
怠無荒如益之所以戒舜也鹽梅舟楫如高宗
之所以望傅說也敬勝怠勝如太公之所以告
武王也君臣之間手足腹心相待一體則感恩
而圖報者咸欲自靖而自獻也况臣子亦素有
忠君愛國之心乘時而思奮者乎由是懷才以
效用者志存乎立功負德以匡時者事專乎報

其時萃淳良核實之能。言下之係乎所率也。漢之三君固非純於王道之主，然而御臣有其道，則臣下之趨向隨之，而况聖明之世，陋三君於不屑者乎？夫君猶盂也，臣猶水也。盂圓則水隨以圓，盂方則水隨以方，惟在陛下一轉移之間耳。

臣願陛下崇寬大之體，廣虛受之衷，委任而相得益章，論道而交儆不替。忠邪當辨，而大臣之細過勿詰可也；事理當審，而言官之狂戇者勿遽震之威可也；罔上當懲也，而事無首尾、泛相沿及者勿槩坐可也；陽是陰非、臆度附會者可誅也，而所見不同、本無意必者勿絶其生還可也。託忠賢以為腹心，開言路以廣耳目。君有匪懈之誠，臣懷媚上之衷。面從後言，如舜之所以戒禹也；無怠無荒，如益之所以戒舜也；鹽梅舟楫，如高宗之所以望傅說也；敬勝怠勝，如太公之所以告武王也。君臣之間，手足腹心，相待一體，則感恩而圖報者咸欲自靖而自獻也，况臣子亦素有忠君愛國之心，乘時而思奮者乎？由是懷才以效用者志存乎立功，負德以匡時者事專乎報
translation_en:
…in his age there gathered men of ability who were honest and upright, examining matters to establish the facts. This means that subordinates depend upon the example of those who lead them. Those three Han rulers were certainly not sovereigns wholly devoted to the Way of the True King. Nevertheless, when they had a proper method of directing their ministers, their ministers’ inclinations followed accordingly. How much more must this be so in an age of sagely enlightenment, which regards those three rulers as too inferior to merit consideration! The ruler is like a basin, and his ministers are like water. If the basin is round, the water takes a round shape; if the basin is square, the water takes a square shape. Everything depends upon a single change of direction by Your Majesty.

Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would uphold a magnanimous manner of rule and broaden your open, receptive heart. Through entrusting responsibilities, let mutual understanding become ever more manifest; through discussing the Way, let mutual admonition never cease. Loyalty and treachery must be distinguished, but it would be proper not to interrogate high ministers over minor faults. The principles of affairs must be carefully examined, but it would be proper not hastily to overawe outspoken and blunt remonstrance officials with your might. Deceiving the sovereign must be punished, but where an affair has no clear beginning or end and people are loosely implicated through their connections, it would be proper not to hold them all indiscriminately guilty. Those who approve openly but disapprove secretly, making conjectures and forcing connections, may deserve execution; yet those whose views differ, but who originally had no willful preconceptions or rigid insistence, should not be deprived of the possibility of returning alive. Entrust loyal and worthy men with service as your closest confidants, and open the channels of remonstrance to extend your eyes and ears. Let the ruler possess sincere, unflagging dedication, and let ministers cherish the desire to please their sovereign. As for assenting to someone’s face but speaking against him afterward, recall how Shun admonished Yu; as for neither growing idle nor neglecting affairs, recall how Yi admonished Shun. As for salt and plums, boats and oars—the indispensable aids to good government—recall what Gaozong expected of Fu Yue. As for whether reverence or indolence prevails, recall what Taigong told King Wu. When ruler and ministers treat one another as hands and feet, belly and heart, belonging to a single body, all those who feel gratitude and seek to repay it will wish to discharge their responsibilities conscientiously and offer their service. How much more will this be true of ministers who have always cherished loyalty to their ruler and love for their country, and who seek to seize the moment to exert themselves! Thus, those who possess talent and offer it in service will set their aspirations on achieving worthy deeds, while those who possess virtue and seek to set the age right will devote their efforts entirely to repaying…

title: 嘉靖三十二年進士登科錄
text:
主廊廟之臣誠篤輔弼省寺之臣誠竭賛襄臺
諫之臣誠盡其言藩臬之臣誠脩其職郡邑之
臣誠效綏牧封疆之臣誠固捍禦脩於家者用
於
天子之廷宣諸言者措諸躬行之實所以翊
陛下垂拱之化者在此矣是猶四時五氣各司其
職而君人者如天運於上不勞而化成者也君
逸臣勞之義豈徒為無實之空言哉雖然知君
逸臣勞之義固當求盡其責然為臣克艱之道
實有未易盡者臣請得而終言之盖昔先王之
===
世以天保以上治内采薇以下治外是以綱紀
畢張而上下並福也然治内者文臣之責治外
者武臣之任今内外之政雖亦同於往古而内
郡黎民之困外地兵政之弊則亦有可言者矣
以民之困言之倉箱無卒歳之儲田里無口分
之業南則病於稅産之虚北則病於邊防之擾
至於災異之地猶失撫字之方封洫溝渠鞠為
草莽仰食待哺之民輾轉而不能自給是以流
離載道攘刼為生則民之窮亦已極矣
陛下特有胞及與之仁而為臣者不能致

===
世以天保以上治內采薇以下治外是以綱紀
畢張而上下並福也然治內者文臣之責治外
者武臣之任今內外之政雖亦同於往古而內
郡黎民之困外地兵政之弊則亦有可言者矣
以民之困言之倉箱無卒歲之儲田里無口分
之業南則病於稅產之虛北則病於邊防之擾
至於災異之地猶失撫字之方封洫溝渠鞠為
草莽仰食待哺之民輾轉而不能自給是以流
離載道擴切為生則民之窮亦已極矣
陛下特由胞及與之仁而為臣者不能致
punctuated:
主。廊廟之臣誠篤輔弼，省寺之臣誠竭賛襄，臺諫之臣誠盡其言，藩臬之臣誠脩其職，郡邑之臣誠效綏牧，封疆之臣誠固捍禦。脩於家者，用於天子之廷；宣諸言者，措諸躬行之實。所以翊陛下垂拱之化者，在此矣。是猶四時五氣各司其職，而君人者如天運於上，不勞而化成者也。君逸臣勞之義，豈徒為無實之空言哉？雖然，知君逸臣勞之義，固當求盡其責，然為臣克艱之道，實有未易盡者。臣請得而終言之。盖昔先王之世，以《天保》以上治内，《采薇》以下治外，是以綱紀畢張，而上下並福也。然治内者，文臣之責；治外者，武臣之任。今内外之政，雖亦同於往古，而内郡黎民之困、外地兵政之弊，則亦有可言者矣。

以民之困言之，倉箱無卒歳之儲，田里無口分之業。南則病於稅産之虚，北則病於邊防之擾。至於災異之地，猶失撫字之方，封洫溝渠鞠為草莽，仰食待哺之民，輾轉而不能自給。是以流離載道，攘刼為生，則民之窮亦已極矣。陛下特有胞及與之仁，而為臣者不能致
translation_en:
…their sovereign. Ministers at court sincerely devote themselves to assisting and advising; those in ministries and courts sincerely exert themselves in support; censors and remonstrance officials sincerely speak their minds fully; provincial administration and surveillance officials sincerely discharge their duties; prefectural and county officials sincerely work to pacify and nurture the people; and frontier officials sincerely strengthen their defenses. What they cultivate at home they put to use at the Son of Heaven’s court; what they proclaim in words they put into actual personal practice. Herein lies their assistance to Your Majesty’s transforming rule, exercised with folded hands. This is like the four seasons and the five vital forces each performing their proper functions, while the ruler of men, like Heaven moving above, brings transformation to completion without toil. How could the principle that the ruler rests while his ministers labor be merely empty words without substance?

Nevertheless, understanding this principle certainly requires ministers to seek to fulfill their responsibilities; yet the way of meeting the difficulties of ministerial service is truly not easily fulfilled. Your servant asks leave to conclude by speaking of this. In the age of the former kings, the poems through Heaven Protects You (Tianbao) served to govern internal affairs, and those from Gathering Bracken (Caiwei) onward served to govern external affairs. Thus the entire framework of government was established, and superiors and inferiors alike enjoyed its blessings. Governing internal affairs, however, was the responsibility of civil officials, while governing external affairs was the charge of military officials. Today, although the administration of internal and external affairs resembles that of antiquity, there is still much to be said about the hardships of the common people in the interior prefectures and the defects of military administration in the outlying regions.

As for the people’s hardships, their granaries and bins hold no reserves sufficient to last the year, and their villages have no landed holdings sufficient to provide each person’s subsistence. In the south they suffer from assessments on property that exists only on paper [?]; in the north they suffer from the disruptions of frontier defense. In places afflicted by disasters and anomalies, moreover, proper measures to care for the people are still lacking. Field boundaries, ditches, and canals have all become overgrown with weeds. People who look to others for food and await relief wander about, unable to support themselves. Consequently, displaced people fill the roads and resort to robbery for their livelihood. The people’s destitution has indeed reached its utmost extreme. Your Majesty possesses a singular benevolence that embraces the people as siblings and all things as companions, yet your ministers are unable to bring…

title: 嘉靖三十二年進士登科錄
text:
國家於民康物阜之化甚非所以仰承克艱之意
也更化善治者尚當求先王治内之政乎必也
重守令之選節浮冗之費時撫字之恩夫
國家所以敷德意而拯捄民瘼者惟守令耳守令
得人則承流宣化可以恤民情之隱浮冗既節
則食寡用舒可以裕財賦之源撫字以時則惠
溥情聯可以固一體之愛如是而民生日厚民
行日興暖衣飽食之衆皆有勇知方之徒也以
兵之弊言之勾稽有冊矣而行伍則虛簡閱有
規矣而老弱如故校練有期而朽甲鈍兵無以
===
當折衝之需侵兵有禁而私役專利不足以一
效死之心是以内地空虛邊庭弛備北虜縱橫
而縮頸股栗盜賊竊發掩耳而不願聽則兵之
弊亦云甚矣
陛下思患預防軫念於四夷之守而為臣者不能為
萬全之謀
國家所以委任典兵之謀為臣所以業官盡職之
道皆不如此也捄弊以壯國者尚當求先王治
外之政乎必也重將帥之選慎教習之法嚴冒
濫之刑夫將帥之任

punctuated:
國家於民康物阜之化，甚非所以仰承克艱之意也。更化善治者，尚當求先王治内之政乎？必也重守令之選，節浮冗之費，時撫字之恩。夫國家所以敷德意而拯捄民瘼者，惟守令耳。守令得人，則承流宣化，可以恤民情之隱；浮冗既節，則食寡用舒，可以裕財賦之源；撫字以時，則惠溥情聯，可以固一體之愛。如是而民生日厚，民行日興，暖衣飽食之衆，皆有勇知方之徒也。
以兵之弊言之，勾稽有冊矣，而行伍則虛；簡閱有規矣，而老弱如故；校練有期，而朽甲鈍兵無以當折衝之需；侵兵有禁，而私役專利不足以一效死之心。是以内地空虛，邊庭弛備，北虜縱橫而縮頸股栗，盜賊竊發，掩耳而不願聽，則兵之弊亦云甚矣。陛下思患預防，軫念於四夷之守，而為臣者不能為萬全之謀。國家所以委任典兵之謀，為臣所以業官盡職之道，皆不如此也。捄弊以壯國者，尚當求先王治外之政乎？必也重將帥之選，慎教習之法，嚴冒濫之刑。夫將帥之任，
translation_en:
…bring the state to a condition in which the people are secure and goods abundant. This gravely fails to honor Your Majesty’s intention to shoulder the difficulties of rule. Should not those who would reform government and govern well seek the former kings’ policies for domestic administration? They must give weight to the selection of prefects and magistrates, curb superfluous expenditures, and provide timely benevolent care for the people. For it is precisely prefects and magistrates through whom the state extends its virtuous intentions and relieves the people’s suffering. If suitable men hold these posts, they can carry forward imperial beneficence and spread its transforming influence, attending to the people’s hidden distress. Once superfluous expenses are curtailed, fewer will consume public resources and funds will be less strained, thereby enriching the sources of revenue. When care is timely, benefits will spread widely and bonds of feeling grow close, strengthening the love that unites ruler and people as one body. Thus the people’s livelihood will grow more substantial each day, and their conduct improve. All those warmly clothed and well fed will possess courage and understand the proper course of conduct.
As for the abuses in military affairs, there are registers for checking the rolls, yet the ranks are empty; there are regulations for inspection, yet the old and weak remain as before. Training takes place at set times, yet rotting armor and blunt weapons cannot meet the needs of repelling an enemy. Abuses against soldiers [?] are prohibited, yet employing them for private service and monopolizing profits fail to unite them in the resolve to fight to the death. Consequently, the interior is depleted and frontier defenses are neglected. When the northern barbarians range unchecked, men draw in their necks and their thighs tremble; when bandits suddenly rise, they cover their ears and refuse to listen. The abuses in military affairs may indeed be called extreme. Your Majesty anticipates dangers and takes precautions, anxiously considering defense against the barbarians on all four sides, yet your servants cannot devise a wholly adequate plan. This accords neither with the state’s purpose in entrusting men with military command nor with the way in which servants of the throne should attend to their offices and fulfill their duties. Should not those who would remedy abuses and strengthen the state seek the former kings’ policies for external affairs? They must give weight to the selection of generals, exercise care over methods of instruction and training, and strictly punish fraudulent claims and indiscriminate appointments. As for the responsibility entrusted to generals…

translation_en:
…is that through which the Son of Heaven entrusts weighty responsibilities, relies upon military strength, and upholds the state's imposing authority. If suitable men are chosen as commanders, these trusted defenders can bear the charge of securing the realm and repelling outsiders. If training is carefully attended to at the proper times, coordinated marching and halting [?] can prepare the troops to counter enemy attacks. If fraudulent and indiscriminate enrollment is punished, the ranks will be filled with brave and vigorous men, remedying their weakness and exhaustion. Thus discipline will be strict and clear, and the state's might will grow daily. The men bearing shields and spears and wearing armor and helmets will all serve as bulwarks defending the state. When internal and external governance are pursued together, without favoring either, civil and military officials will put into practice and personally embody the means of fulfilling their arduous responsibilities.
Your Majesty extends the virtue of Heaven and Earth and keeps the people in mind; your assembled ministers accept the weighty trust placed in them and render loyal service to their sovereign. If sovereign and ministers each fulfill their proper duties, beneficence will spread daily and moral instruction will abound. There will be no difficulty in bringing all the people of this age into a realm of benevolence and longevity. How, then, could the transforming rule that brings peace and order be beyond attainment as Your Majesty sits with folded hands in the depths of the palace? Yet the sovereign's desire for good government is inexhaustible, and his servants' love for their ruler has no end. I have already fully discussed the state's means of directing its ministers and policies suited to the times. As for the fundamental essentials, your servant ventures to offer a further explanation. Your servant has heard these words of Confucius: “The conduct of government depends upon men; the selection of men depends upon one's own person.” Dong Zhongshu said: “The ruler rectifies his heart in order to rectify the court; he rectifies the court in order to rectify the hundred officials; he rectifies the hundred officials in order to rectify the myriad people.” Both mean that the ruler's own heart is the foundation for employing men.
Your Majesty carries forward the transmission of the learning of the mind and reveals the mysteries of the succession of the Way. As you remain composed and silent in the depths of the palace, nurturing the mind's empty, luminous, tranquil, and unified essence, then…

title: 嘉靖三十二年進士登科錄
text:
聖心之純固足為照臨百官之本矣然慎終如始尤
聖心之所宜留念者臣願
陛下於宫闈深邃之中𣣔氣清明之際靜虛動直以
植乎此心之本察識擴充以達乎此心之用使
天理常明私欲淨盡則心無不正身無不脩而
取人之本正矣由是而乗興清明羣邪不能為
之惑權度精切眾說不能為之淆取舎不以系於
愛憎賞罰不狥於喜怒猶鑑之照物妍媸之在彼
隨物而自應者也百官之正萬民之正一惟涵
養此心之所運耳四海之內又孰不聞盛徳而
===
来臣哉臣也尋章摘句非有正大不易之論然
而狂瞽之見始以御臣之道為
陛下告終以取人之本為
陛下勉惟以明諸其心上不負
陛下下不負所學而已惟
陛下矜憫愚誠而留神嘉納臣不勝戰兢隕越之至
臣謹對

聖心之純固足為照臨百官之本矣。然慎終如始，尤聖心之所宜留念者。臣願陛下於宫闈深邃之中，𣣔氣清明之際，靜虛動直，以植乎此心之本；察識擴充，以達乎此心之用。使天理常明，私欲淨盡，則心無不正，身無不脩，而取人之本正矣。由是而乗興清明，羣邪不能為之惑；權度精切，眾說不能為之淆。取舎不以系於愛憎，賞罰不狥於喜怒，猶鑑之照物，妍媸之在彼，隨物而自應者也。百官之正，萬民之正，一惟涵養此心之所運耳。四海之內，又孰不聞盛徳而来臣哉？
臣也尋章摘句，非有正大不易之論。然而狂瞽之見，始以御臣之道為陛下告，終以取人之本為陛下勉，惟以明諸其心，上不負陛下，下不負所學而已。惟陛下矜憫愚誠，而留神嘉納。臣不勝戰兢隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…the purity of Your Majesty’s sagely mind is assuredly sufficient to serve as the foundation for illuminating and overseeing the hundred officials. Yet remaining as vigilant at the end as at the beginning especially deserves Your Majesty’s attention. Your servant wishes that, deep within the palace, when desires and vital energies are clear [?], Your Majesty would remain empty of preconceptions in stillness and upright in action, thereby establishing the foundation of this mind; and would discern and extend its moral awareness, thereby fully realizing its operation. Let heavenly principle remain ever bright and selfish desires be utterly purged. Then the mind will be entirely rectified and the person fully cultivated, and the foundation for selecting men will be set right. From this, clarity will prevail [?], and the many wicked will be unable to mislead you; your standards of judgment will be exact, and competing opinions will be unable to confuse them. Selection and rejection will not depend upon affection or aversion, nor will rewards and punishments follow pleasure or anger. It will be like a mirror reflecting things: beauty and ugliness belong to the things themselves, and the mirror responds spontaneously to each. The rectification of the hundred officials and of the myriad people depends entirely upon the workings of this cultivated mind. Within the Four Seas, who would hear of your magnificent virtue and fail to come and acknowledge himself your subject?
Your servant merely searches out passages and picks out phrases; I have no discourse that is truly upright, great, and unalterable. Nevertheless, in offering these rash and benighted views, I began by addressing Your Majesty on the way to govern ministers and ended by exhorting Your Majesty concerning the foundation for selecting men. I seek only to make these matters clear in my own mind, so that, above, I do not fail Your Majesty and, below, I do not betray what I have learned. May Your Majesty take pity on my foolish sincerity, give these words your attention, and graciously accept them. Your servant is overwhelmed with trembling fear, apprehensive that I may stumble and fall. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖三十二年進士登科錄
text:
臣曹大章
臣對臣聞人君法天道而端拱於上有以操天
下之大權人臣代天工而効忠於下有以宣天
下之大化君者奉天之意宰制民物之命者也
故事天如父臣者承君之委協理民物之紀者
也故事君如天君惟以天道御臣也於是攬乾
剛之斷秉離照之明辨賢否之分嚴威賞之施
巍然若天體之運於上而民和物阜端黙以享
其成功臣惟以天道事君也於是竭忠貞之節
效股肱之力盡代終之義致委身之誠儼然若
===
天威之臨於下而仁民愛物精白以承其休徳
君享其成則逸於任人者非以自安也實君之
道也君而不知所以自逸是下無臣職而非克
艱厥君者矣臣承其休則勞於任事者非以自
瘁也實臣之職也臣而不知所以自勞是上負
君命而非克艱厥臣者矣然上有神聖之君而
下或鮮忠藎之臣亦惟明以辨之剛以斷之端
本原以導其趨持紀法以肅其度則內外臣工
罔不淬礪以盡職洗滌以從事由是而明良之
會以啓由是而雍熙之化以成而恢恢乎上古

臣對：臣聞人君法天道而端拱於上，有以操天下之大權；人臣代天工而効忠於下，有以宣天下之大化。君者，奉天之意，宰制民物之命者也，故事天如父；臣者，承君之委，協理民物之紀者也，故事君如天。君惟以天道御臣也，於是攬乾剛之斷，秉離照之明，辨賢否之分，嚴威賞之施，巍然若天體之運於上，而民和物阜，端黙以享其成功。臣惟以天道事君也，於是竭忠貞之節，效股肱之力，盡代終之義，致委身之誠，儼然若天威之臨於下，而仁民愛物，精白以承其休徳。君享其成，則逸於任人者，非以自安也，實君之道也。君而不知所以自逸，是下無臣職，而非克艱厥君者矣。臣承其休，則勞於任事者，非以自瘁也，實臣之職也。臣而不知所以自勞，是上負君命，而非克艱厥臣者矣。然上有神聖之君，而下或鮮忠藎之臣，亦惟明以辨之，剛以斷之，端本原以導其趨，持紀法以肅其度，則內外臣工罔不淬礪以盡職，洗滌以從事。由是而明良之會以啓，由是而雍熙之化以成，而恢恢乎上古
translation_en:
Your servant, Cao Dazhang.

Your servant replies: I have heard that the ruler models himself on the Way of Heaven and sits upright with hands folded above, thereby holding the great authority over all under Heaven. His ministers carry out Heaven’s work and render loyal service below, thereby extending its great transforming influence throughout the realm. The ruler reverently follows Heaven’s intent and governs the destinies of the people and all things; thus he serves Heaven as his father. Ministers accept the ruler’s charge and assist in ordering the affairs of the people and all things; thus they serve the ruler as Heaven.

The ruler governs his ministers through the Way of Heaven. Accordingly, he exercises the decisive firmness of Qian and possesses the illuminating clarity of Li, distinguishes the worthy from the unworthy, and rigorously administers punishments and rewards. Majestic as the movements of the heavens above, he enjoys the accomplishments of his government in upright silence, while the people live in harmony and all things flourish. Ministers serve their ruler through the Way of Heaven. Accordingly, they fulfill their duty of loyal steadfastness, exert themselves as his limbs, discharge their obligation to bring his undertakings to completion, and offer the sincerity of complete personal dedication. Solemn as Heaven’s majesty descending below, they show benevolence to the people and care for all things, sustaining his splendid virtue with purity of purpose.

The ruler enjoys their accomplishments: his ease through entrusting tasks to others is not a pursuit of personal comfort, but is indeed the proper way of a ruler. If a ruler does not understand how to secure this ease, those below have no ministerial duties to fulfill, and he cannot be said to recognize the difficulty of being a ruler. Ministers sustain his excellence: their toil in undertaking affairs is not an effort merely to wear themselves out, but is indeed their proper duty. If a minister does not understand how to exert himself, he fails the ruler’s charge from above and cannot be said to recognize the difficulty of being a minister.

Yet even when there is a sagely ruler above, loyal and devoted ministers below may be few. He need only distinguish them with clear discernment, decide their cases with firmness, rectify the foundations to guide their inclinations, and uphold rules and laws to enforce proper conduct. Then officials both at court and outside it will all sharpen themselves to fulfill their duties and cleanse themselves to undertake their work. Through this, the meeting of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers will be brought about; through this, the transforming influence of harmony and prosperity will be achieved, and vast indeed will be the high antiquity’s …

之治矣欽惟
皇帝陛下
秉天縱之資
乘日中之運蘊離明以照物奮乾剛以用權敬
天而玄德格於
昊穹勤民而仁恩沛於海宇所謂唐虞之盛治堯舜
之盛王蓋兼有之矣生今之世爲今之臣有不
思盡忠畢力以報効於明時者必其無血氣者
也况
王者壽考以作人
===
聖人久道而成化而草茅賤士涵濡樂育有年於兹
敢不拜
明問而罄一得之愚乎臣聞之天道不言而歲功
成者何謂也四時之吏五行之佐宣其氣矣聖
人不言而治化弘者何謂也六卿分職百官率

二氣之運五行之布無非上天之事二氣五行

太和無非上天之功君者其尊猶之天也臣者
其卑猶之二氣五行也故王者法天之陽以生

之治矣。欽惟皇帝陛下，秉天縱之資，乘日中之運，蘊離明以照物，奮乾剛以用權，敬天而玄德格於昊穹，勤民而仁恩沛於海宇。所謂唐虞之盛治、堯舜之盛王，蓋兼有之矣。生今之世，爲今之臣，有不思盡忠畢力以報効於明時者，必其無血氣者也。况王者壽考以作人，聖人久道而成化，而草茅賤士涵濡樂育有年於兹，敢不拜明問而罄一得之愚乎？

臣聞之：天道不言而歲功成者，何謂也？四時之吏、五行之佐宣其氣矣。聖人不言而治化弘者，何謂也？六卿分職，百官率屬，張其教矣。故天運於上，未嘗見其有所事，而二氣之運、五行之布，無非上天之事。二氣五行未嘗敢自言其功，而物之性命各正，運之保合太和，無非上天之功。君者，其尊猶之天也；臣者，其卑猶之二氣五行也。故王者法天之陽以生

…the governance of high antiquity would thus be realized. Reverently considering Your Majesty the Emperor: endowed with Heaven-bestowed gifts, you preside over an age like the sun at its zenith. You harbor the brightness of Li to illuminate all things and rouse the strength of Qian to exercise authority. In revering Heaven, your profound virtue reaches the highest heavens; in diligently caring for the people, your benevolent favor pours forth throughout the realm. The flourishing government of Tang and Yu and the sagely kingship of Yao and Shun may indeed both be found in you. Anyone born in this age and serving as a minister today who does not think of exhausting his loyalty and strength in service to this enlightened age must surely be devoid of living feeling. Moreover, the king enjoys longevity and nurtures men of talent; the sage perseveres in the Way and brings moral transformation to completion. Having for years been steeped in this influence and graciously nurtured, how could a humble scholar from the countryside such as I dare fail to receive your illuminating question reverently and offer the utmost of my meager understanding?

Your servant has heard this: what does it mean that Heaven's Way does not speak, yet the year's work is accomplished? The officials of the four seasons and the assistants of the Five Phases disseminate its vital energy. What does it mean that the sage does not speak, yet orderly government and moral transformation spread widely? The six ministers divide their duties, and the hundred officials lead their subordinates, extending his teaching. Thus Heaven moves above, and though it is never seen attending to any business, the circulation of the two vital energies and the distribution of the Five Phases are all Heaven's work. The two energies and Five Phases never dare claim merit for themselves; yet each thing attains its proper nature and allotted existence, and their movement preserves and unites supreme harmony [?]—all of this is Heaven's achievement. The ruler's exalted position resembles Heaven's; the ministers' lowly position resembles that of the two energies and Five Phases. Thus the king models himself upon Heaven's yang to bring forth…

title: 嘉靖三十二年進士登科錄
text:
萬物而張之文吏以修其文教焉法天之陰以
肅萬物而置之武吏以奮其武衞焉君人法天
之運操其御文御武之權若太極之均節乎陰
陽而安享其文修武偃之功焉是其恭已南面
在君不言逸胼手胝足在臣不言勞以上御下
以卑承尊皆效法於天地而取義於陰陽理之
一定道之自然者也昔者禹謨曰后克艱厥后
臣克艱厥臣自今考之堯以欽明之德臨于上
史稱其垂衣而治而有若禹平水土稷教稼穡
舜職百揆羲和授時堯之事固羣臣受其責矣
===
舜以濬哲之德臨于上史稱其無爲而治而有
若伯夷典禮后夔典樂皐陶明刑以正猾夏大
禹勤兵以征有苗而舜之爲羣臣固代其終矣
當其時元首股肱猶之一人而庶民萬物聯之
一體心在君父不敢以私其身事在社稷不敢
以私其家百僚相師相讓以各獻其能於天子
位苟當其才雖卑瑣之賤終身居之而無覬覦
之心人苟賢於已雖側陋之微誠心揚之而無
忌嫉之意稷勤於播種不耻其不能教而視契
之敷教猶已之能也夷勤於典禮不耻其不通

萬物，而張之文吏，以修其文教焉；法天之陰以肅萬物，而置之武吏，以奮其武衞焉。君人法天之運，操其御文御武之權，若太極之均節乎陰陽，而安享其文修武偃之功焉。是其恭已南面，在君不言逸；胼手胝足，在臣不言勞。以上御下，以卑承尊，皆效法於天地，而取義於陰陽，理之一定、道之自然者也。
昔者《禹謨》曰：「后克艱厥后，臣克艱厥臣。」自今考之，堯以欽明之德臨于上，史稱其垂衣而治，而有若禹平水土，稷教稼穡，舜職百揆，羲和授時，堯之事固羣臣受其責矣。舜以濬哲之德臨于上，史稱其無爲而治，而有若伯夷典禮，后夔典樂，皐陶明刑以正猾夏，大禹勤兵以征有苗，而舜之爲，羣臣固代其終矣。
當其時，元首股肱猶之一人，而庶民萬物聯之一體。心在君父，不敢以私其身；事在社稷，不敢以私其家。百僚相師相讓，以各獻其能於天子。位苟當其才，雖卑瑣之賤，終身居之而無覬覦之心；人苟賢於已，雖側陋之微，誠心揚之而無忌嫉之意。稷勤於播種，不耻其不能教，而視契之敷教猶已之能也；夷勤於典禮，不耻其不通

The ruler of men models himself on Heaven’s movements and holds the authority to direct both civil and military affairs, just as the Supreme Ultimate balances and regulates yin and yang. Thus he peacefully enjoys the achievement of flourishing civil government and arms laid to rest. Comporting himself reverently and facing south, the ruler does not speak of ease; with calloused hands and feet, his ministers do not speak of toil. Those above direct those below, and those of lower station serve the exalted. All model themselves on Heaven and Earth and derive their principles from yin and yang: this is the fixed order of principle and the natural course of the Way.
In ancient times, the Counsels of Yu stated: “Let the sovereign recognize the difficulty of being sovereign, and ministers recognize the difficulty of being ministers.” Examining this from our own day, Yao presided above with reverence and enlightened virtue. The histories say that he governed merely by letting his robes hang down. Yet there were men such as Yu, who brought the waters and lands into order; Ji, who taught sowing and reaping; Shun, who oversaw the hundred offices; and Xi and He, who determined the seasons. Yao’s ministers indeed assumed responsibility for his affairs. Shun presided above with profound wisdom. The histories say that he governed without acting. Yet there were men such as Bo Yi, who supervised rites; Hou Kui, who supervised music; Gao Yao, who clarified punishments to correct those who disrupted the Xia realm; and the great Yu, who marshaled troops to campaign against the Youmiao. Shun’s ministers indeed brought his undertakings to completion on his behalf.
At that time, the head and the limbs—the ruler and his ministers—were like a single person, while the common people and all things were joined into one body. With their hearts devoted to their ruler and father, they dared not pursue private advantage for themselves; with their labors devoted to the altars of soil and grain, they dared not pursue private advantage for their families. The hundred officials learned from and deferred to one another, each offering his abilities to the Son of Heaven. If an office suited a man’s talents, however lowly and insignificant it might be, he would occupy it throughout his life without coveting another. If someone surpassed him in worth, however humble and obscure that person might be, he would sincerely promote him without jealousy. title: 嘉靖三十二年進士登科錄
text:
樂而視夔之典樂猶己之能也其視天下之人
皆若一人之身耳之所涉目必效焉手之所持
足必前焉志意浹洽精神流貫癢疴呼吸感觸
神應真若天地殊位陰陽異行而其中一氣翕
闢相交相濟以成歲功民物豐阜天下太和而
堯舜有以享雍熈之盛成大同之治者良有以
也下逮漢唐宋風氣漸漓人心不古君具典章
法度之文不足以統馭人紀而無乾斷之剛臣
務議論聲容之美不足以縁飾治功而鮮坤承
之實亦由其所尚不審雜夷雜覇上下皆隨世
苟且以就事功無恠乎其治之不振矣洪惟
太祖高皇帝復宇宙千古綱常之治定臣民萬世紀
法之宗有劉宋諸臣以修其文有徐常諸臣以
燿其武混一區宇底定太平雖神謀睿算
聖心之獨運而戮力奏功則羣臣之代終者也
列聖相承至我
皇上妙道凝於性成
至德粹於神授體乾之剛健中正法堯之文武聖
神以續千載不傳之道統以修歷代未備之禮
制以用天付一世之人材以振

樂，而視夔之典樂猶己之能也。其視天下之人，皆若一人之身：耳之所涉，目必效焉；手之所持，足必前焉。志意浹洽，精神流貫，癢疴呼吸，感觸神應，真若天地殊位、陰陽異行，而其中一氣翕闢，相交相濟，以成歲功。民物豐阜，天下太和，而堯舜有以享雍熈之盛、成大同之治者，良有以也。
下逮漢唐宋，風氣漸漓，人心不古。君具典章法度之文，不足以統馭人紀，而無乾斷之剛；臣務議論聲容之美，不足以縁飾治功，而鮮坤承之實。亦由其所尚不審，雜夷雜覇，上下皆隨世苟且，以就事功，無恠乎其治之不振矣。

…music, yet regarded Kui’s administration of music as though it were his own ability. They regarded all the people under Heaven as the members of a single body: wherever the ears reached, the eyes would perform their part; whatever the hands held, the feet would advance to support. Their purposes were in complete accord, their vital spirits flowed throughout, and every itch, ache, and breath elicited a wondrous response. It was truly like Heaven and Earth occupying distinct positions, and yin and yang following different courses, while the single vital force within them contracted and expanded, interacting and assisting each other to bring the year’s work to completion. That the people and all things flourished, that all under Heaven enjoyed supreme harmony, and that Yao and Shun could enjoy such abundant peace and accomplish the government of Great Unity—these things indeed had their reasons.
By the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties, prevailing customs had gradually deteriorated, and people’s hearts were no longer as in antiquity. Rulers possessed the outward forms of institutions, regulations, laws, and standards, yet these were insufficient to govern human relationships, and they lacked the firmness of Heaven’s decisiveness. Ministers pursued elegance in discussion, speech, and bearing, yet these were insufficient to embellish the achievements of government, and they had little of the substance of Earth’s supportive obedience. This, too, arose because they failed to examine carefully what they esteemed, mixing in barbarian ways and the methods of hegemonic rule. High and low alike drifted with the times and expediently sought results. Little wonder that their government failed to flourish.
We reverently reflect that Emperor Taizu Gao restored throughout the universe the government of the enduring cardinal relationships and constant virtues, and established for officials and people the fundamental standards of order and law for all ages. Ministers such as Liu and Song cultivated his civil achievements; ministers such as Xu and Chang made his military achievements shine. He unified the realm and firmly established peace. Although the wondrous plans and sagacious calculations proceeded solely from his imperial mind, it was his assembled ministers who joined their efforts to achieve success and carried his work through to completion.
The sage emperors succeeded one another down to Our Sovereign. The wondrous Way is firmly embodied in his innate nature, and his supreme virtue is pure through divine bestowal. He embodies Heaven’s strength, vigor, centrality, and correctness, and takes as his model Yao’s civil and military accomplishments, sagacity, and spiritual insight, thereby continuing the succession of the Way left untransmitted for a thousand years, perfecting the ritual institutions left incomplete by successive dynasties, employing the talented men whom Heaven has bestowed upon this age, and revitalizing…

text:

郊壇之祀則有
欽天記頌之作定耕桑之制則有蠶壇穀祗之賦何
如其敬
天也念窮貧之疾則有藥餌之惠聞饑荒之奏則有
銀粟之賑何如其勤民也是身雖居乎
九重而慮則周於四海位雖齊乎
宸極而情則通乎閭閻其在小民之休戚涖其事者
或未察其詳而
宸衷已徹其幾微其屬邊境之利害臨其地者或未
===
核其實而
睿照已燭其幽隱故一賞罰天下仰之如神明而以
勸以懲一號令天下奉之如風霆而以鼓以舞
古有所謂君逸臣勞者而臣竊知
陛下身雖逸而心則勞而憂勤圖治之誠較之諸臣

祖垂萬年之綱紀。秩郊壇之祀，則有《欽天記頌》之作；定耕桑之制，則有蠶壇、穀祗之賦。何如其敬天也！念窮貧之疾，則有藥餌之惠；聞饑荒之奏，則有銀粟之賑。何如其勤民也！是身雖居乎九重，而慮則周於四海；位雖齊乎宸極，而情則通乎閭閻。其在小民之休戚，涖其事者或未察其詳，而宸衷已徹其幾微；其屬邊境之利害，臨其地者或未核其實，而睿照已燭其幽隱。故一賞罰，天下仰之如神明，而以勸以懲；一號令，天下奉之如風霆，而以鼓以舞。

古有所謂君逸臣勞者，而臣竊知陛下身雖逸，而心則勞，而憂勤圖治之誠，較之諸臣，殆尤有獨甚者也。夫一心所向，百體効力；一人所指，百司爭先，虞廷所以有從欲之治也。而今九重之上，既先以憂勤率下矣，復一有微能，則名器有所不愛，而寵綏天下之文臣；一有微功，則節鉞有所不靳，而大賚天下之武士。內外臣工固

…the guiding principles bequeathed by the imperial ancestor for ten thousand years. When Your Majesty ordered the sacrifices at the suburban altars, you composed the Record and Eulogy of Revering Heaven; when you established the regulations for plowing and sericulture, you composed rhapsodies on the Silkworm Altar and the Grain Deity. How profound is your reverence for Heaven! Mindful of the illnesses of the destitute, you bestowed medicines; upon hearing reports of famine, you supplied relief in silver and grain. How devoted is your care for the people! Though your person resides within the ninefold palace, your thoughts encompass all within the Four Seas; though your position equals the celestial pole in height, your sympathies reach the common people's lanes. In matters affecting ordinary people's welfare and suffering, those administering their affairs may not yet have examined the details, yet the imperial mind has already penetrated their slightest indications. In matters concerning benefits and dangers along the frontiers, those stationed there may not yet have verified the facts, yet your sagely discernment has already illuminated what lies hidden. Thus, whenever you confer a reward or impose a punishment, all under Heaven look up to you as to a divine power, receiving encouragement or chastening; whenever you issue a command, all under Heaven obey it as they would wind and thunder, stirred and inspired.

The ancients spoke of the ruler being at ease while his ministers labored. Yet your servant humbly knows that, although Your Majesty's body may be at ease, your mind labors. Indeed, the sincerity of your anxious diligence in seeking good government probably far exceeds that of all your ministers. Wherever the single mind directs itself, the body's hundred parts exert their strength; wherever the One Man points, the hundred offices vie to act first. text:
紆外捍之慮
皇上端冕服之垂儼黼扆之御妙淵微之敬操總攬
之權若天之穆然運於上而萬姓羣然其樂生
焉萬物熙然其時育焉此
今日治功之盛而天下所快覩者也雖然持節剖
符膺民社之責而爲文吏者何限也內之所以
順治者係於此也推轂授鉞受邊境之委而爲
武吏者何限也外之所以威嚴者係於此也顧
瘝官廢事者恒不絕聞而効忠宣力者槩不多
見曾不一思曰上之所以寵我以爵位者將有
===
以責我也而假之爲威赫之具惠我以廩禄者
將有以用我也而借之爲聚斂之媒古者民賴
官以爲生今者聽民之自生聽其自生可矣又
從而科求之民苦于剥膚之虐何以責其安土
古者兵待將以爲給今者聽兵之自給聽其自
給可矣又從而浚削之兵病于枵腹之瘠何以
責其力戰吏以安郡邑今不惟無以安之而所
以危郡邑者吏實爲之也將以强邊境今不惟
無以强之而所以弱邊境者將實爲之也是以
在內多流離瑣尾之民而腹心之元氣不實在

…to ease concerns about defense against external threats. Your Majesty wears the pendant crown and ceremonial robes with dignity and sits in solemn majesty before the embroidered screen of the throne. You perfect a reverence profound and subtle, and wield the authority that comprehends all affairs. Like Heaven moving in silent majesty above, you enable the myriad people together to delight in life and all things to flourish, each growing in its season. Such is the splendor of today’s achievements in government, which all under Heaven rejoice to behold.
Nevertheless, how numerous are the civil officials who bear credentials of authority and receive divided tallies of investiture, charged with responsibility for the people and the altars of the soil! Upon them depends orderly government within the realm. How numerous are the military officials who are sent forth with the ceremonial pushing of their chariot wheels and granted battle-axes of command, entrusted with the frontier! Upon them depends the awe commanded abroad. Yet reports of officials neglecting their offices and abandoning their duties never cease, while those who exert themselves loyally in service are, on the whole, seldom seen. They never once reflect: “The sovereign honors me with rank and position because he intends to hold me accountable.” Instead, they turn these into instruments of intimidation. He favors them with official stipends because he intends to employ their services, yet they use these as a means of amassing wealth through exactions.
In antiquity, the people relied on officials for their livelihood; now they are left to provide for themselves. Leaving them to provide for themselves might be tolerable, but officials go further and impose levies and demands upon them. When the people suffer from cruelty that strips their very skin, how can they be expected to remain content on their land? In antiquity, soldiers depended on their commanders for supplies; now they are left to supply themselves. Leaving them to supply themselves might be tolerable, but commanders go further and squeeze and fleece them. When soldiers are afflicted by hunger and emaciation, how can they be expected to fight with all their strength?
Officials are appointed to bring peace to prefectures and counties. Now they not only fail to bring them peace: it is the officials themselves who imperil them. Commanders are appointed to strengthen the frontier. Now they not only fail to strengthen it: it is the commanders themselves who weaken it. 以厪

聖諭所謂君逸臣勞先行其言視爲虛語者不盡無
也
陛下亦嘗一察其弊原矣乎盖文治之不飭固由在
位者無廉仁之德而不知其原由於學術之不
正學校者賢才之所出也今飾詞章綴艶藻以
獵取爵位忠孝之理雖日陳於言而未嘗一致
其實焉則見之不明功利足以動其念守之不
===
固富貴足以搖其衷沿習久而以守正者爲要
名蔽錮深而以廉約者爲無術自其就學之初
其志已非而文職之不修不待授之以官而後
見矣
陛下亦惟有以振揚之如古之賓興之典三物之敎
不必盡襲其舊師其意而著之令典示天下知
所嚮風焉至於崇道德以端士尚獎廉退以堅
士節優忠直以振士風加禮遇以隆士體于以
移易其心志洗濯其耳目使其以貪功慕利之
念爲憂君體國之誠則中有定見確然不移内

外多跳梁侵軼之虜，而肢體之神氣不揚，皆有以厪當宁之隱憂者。則聖諭所謂「君逸臣勞」、「先行其言」，視爲虛語者，不盡無也。陛下亦嘗一察其弊原矣乎？盖文治之不飭，固由在位者無廉仁之德，而不知其原由於學術之不正。學校者，賢才之所出也。今飾詞章，綴艶藻，以獵取爵位；忠孝之理，雖日陳於言，而未嘗一致其實焉。則見之不明，功利足以動其念；守之不固，富貴足以搖其衷。沿習久，而以守正者爲要名；蔽錮深，而以廉約者爲無術。自其就學之初，其志已非，而文職之不修，不待授之以官而後見矣。

translation_en:
…beyond the borders, marauding enemies abound, and the vitality of the realm’s limbs fails to rise. All this gives Your Majesty cause for private anxiety. Thus there are indeed those who regard as empty words the principles expressed in your sacred instruction: “The ruler rests at ease while his ministers toil” and “First put one’s words into practice.” Has Your Majesty ever examined the source of these abuses? The disorder of civil government certainly stems from the lack of integrity and benevolence among those in office; yet people fail to recognize that its source lies in misguided learning. Schools are where worthy and talented men emerge. Today, men embellish their compositions and string together florid phrases to hunt down rank and office. Although they speak daily of the principles of loyalty and filial devotion, they never actually put them into practice. Because their understanding is unclear, achievement and profit can stir their desires; because their adherence is insecure, wealth and high station can sway their hearts. Long habituation leads them to regard those who uphold what is right as seekers of reputation; deeply entrenched blindness leads them to regard the incorruptible and frugal as men without practical ability. From the very beginning of their schooling, their ambitions are already misguided. Their failure to discharge civil duties can therefore be discerned even before they receive an official appointment.

Your Majesty must find means to invigorate them. Take, for example, the ancient ceremonies for honoring and recommending worthy men, and instruction in the three categories of virtue, conduct, and skills: there is no need to reproduce all their old forms. Follow their intent and embody it in authoritative regulations, showing everyone under Heaven the example toward which they should turn. Furthermore, exalt moral virtue to rectify scholars’ aspirations; reward integrity and modest withdrawal to strengthen their principles; favor the loyal and upright to invigorate their ethos; and accord them greater ceremonial courtesy to enhance their dignity. In this way, transform their hearts and ambitions and cleanse their ears and eyes. Turn their craving for achievement and profit into sincere concern for their ruler and devotion to the state. Then they will possess settled convictions within, firm and unshakable, whether within…

text:
外常變惟其指使不求吏於吏求吏於養士而
緩急所需天下不患其無文臣武功之不競固
由為將者無捍禦之謀而不知其原由於敎練
之不素世胄者將士之所出也襲紈綺安豢養
以坐待資廕韜鈐之畧雖日陳於言而未嘗一
識其奥焉則養之無術臨難足以嬰其慮講之
不預遇敵足以懾其衷鈆刀不足以膺割而朽
壤不足以為障自其安居之時其氣已索而武
功之不奮不待臨之以陣而後見矣
陛下亦惟有以變通之如古之大射之法大閱之禮
不必盡沿其制師其意而陳之紀律示天下知
所從事焉至於儲之以預其養選之以校其能
任之以盡其才御之以嚴其法于以作新其志
意而鼓舞其精神使以計功謀利之誠為籌邊
慮敵之策則强弱險易洞若指掌千里制勝妙
於一心不求將於將求將於訓胄而緩急所需
天下不患其無武臣此皆拔本塞源之論而今
之時則有未易更定者盖立法久則日趨於弊
而因循深則日忘其非甚至紀綱之虛名僅存
紀綱之實意盡喪猶動委之曰此成法也此舊

武功之不競，固由為將者無捍禦之謀，而不知其原由於敎練之不素。世胄者，將士之所出也。襲紈綺，安豢養，以坐待資廕。韜鈐之畧，雖日陳於言，而未嘗一識其奥焉。則養之無術，臨難足以嬰其慮；講之不預，遇敵足以懾其衷。鈆刀不足以膺割，而朽壤不足以為障。自其安居之時，其氣已索，而武功之不奮，不待臨之以陣而後見矣。
陛下亦惟有以變通之，如古之大射之法、大閱之禮，不必盡沿其制，師其意而陳之紀律，示天下知所從事焉。至於儲之以預其養，選之以校其能，任之以盡其才，御之以嚴其法，于以作新其志意而鼓舞其精神，使以計功謀利之誠為籌邊慮敵之策，則强弱險易，洞若指掌；千里制勝，妙於一心。不求將於將，求將於訓胄，而緩急所需，天下不患其無武臣。

…external affairs, ordinary circumstances and unforeseen changes—all will respond to their direction. Seek officials through the cultivation of scholars, rather than among officials themselves, and the realm need not fear a lack of civil officials to meet its needs, whether routine or urgent.
The failure of military achievements to flourish certainly stems from commanders’ lack of plans for defense. Yet people fail to recognize that its source lies in the absence of prior instruction and training. Descendants of hereditary military families are the source of commanders and soldiers. Clad in fine silks and content to be maintained in comfort, they sit waiting to inherit positions through ancestral privilege. Though military strategy is discussed daily, they have never gained any understanding of its subtleties. When their upbringing lacks proper methods, danger entangles their thoughts; when they have not trained beforehand, encountering the enemy strikes fear into their hearts. A leaden blade cannot perform the work of cutting, nor can crumbling earth serve as a defensive barrier. Even while they dwell at ease, their vigor is already exhausted. Their inability to achieve military success can be seen without waiting to put them into battle.
Your Majesty need only devise ways to reform these practices. Take, for example, the ancient institutions of the Great Archery Ceremony and the rituals of the Grand Military Review: there is no need to follow their forms in every detail. Emulate their intent and embody it in regulations, so that all under Heaven know what they should undertake. Maintain a reserve of men to provide for their nurture in advance; select them by assessing their abilities; employ them so that their talents are fully exercised; and command them through strict enforcement of the rules. In this way, renew their aspirations and rouse their spirits. Turn the earnestness with which they calculate achievements and seek advantage toward plans for the frontier and deliberations concerning the enemy. Then relative strength and weakness, difficult and easy terrain, will be as clear to them as their own palms; the subtle art of securing victory a thousand li away will reside in a single mind. Seek commanders through the training of hereditary military descendants, rather than among commanders themselves, and the realm need not fear a lack of military officials to meet its needs, whether routine or urgent.
These arguments all address the roots and sources of the problem. Yet under present circumstances, some things cannot readily be altered and settled anew. When institutions have stood for a long time, they become more prone to abuses by the day; as habitual compliance deepens, people increasingly forget what is wrong with them. Matters reach the point where scarcely the empty name of governing order remains, while its substance and purpose have been entirely lost. …precedent.” Those holding higher office follow these precedents as rules of qualification and seniority, thereby obscuring whether men are worthy or unworthy; those holding lower office adhere to them in their official correspondence, thereby confusing sincerity with deceit. Those in charge treat their offices as relay stations, while those seeking advancement take bribery and connections as shortcuts. The means by which the ruler holds the reins and sets all under Heaven in motion are simply official titles and insignia, rewards and punishments. If these are not used to scrutinize men’s actual moral character, achievements, and abilities, but business is conducted solely through perfunctory paperwork, how can one expect them to discharge their offices properly?

Moreover, those who harm the realm are its generals and officials; what leads the realm’s generals and officials astray is its statutes and precedents. When laws reach an impasse, they must change; with change comes a way forward. Certainly, one need not make disruptive changes that throw established regulations into confusion; yet neither may one grow lax and allow corruption to flourish. Furthermore, in the present condition of the realm, the pursuit of gain has penetrated people’s minds so deeply, and habits of frivolity and extravagance have persisted so long, that they resemble a disease lodged in the vital organs. Unless a sage physician washes out the bowels and stomach and removes the accumulated poisons, there can be little hope of restoring health.

When a physician tries a prescription and it proves ineffective, he still considers another course. In past years, famine afflicted the southeast and barbarian raiders attacked the northwest; local officials and frontier ministers stood helpless, without a plan. Thus the measures already tried have proved ineffective. Yet if there is still no change of course to rouse them from their decline, what they will accomplish year after year can be known simply by looking at their past conduct. How, then, can they bring matters to a satisfactory conclusion? Instead of attending to prevention before trouble arises, they merely create commotion when it comes: today adding an official, tomorrow issuing an edict. Such petty and incessant changes ill befit the dignity of the state; and as people grow accustomed to seeing and hearing them, they become mere formalities. These are all remedies for particular defects and abuses, not policies for enduring peace and lasting good government.
